rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses imposed on Sāmiri lifelong social exclusion as a punishment for hypocrisy, which Islahi calls moral leprosy and filthier than physical leprosy.
rows.anchor: for S āmir ī it was a life-long punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’anic humiliation is sharpened by comparison with the Torah's leper rule: declaring oneself unclean is the ultimate humiliation.
rows.anchor: the ultimate of extent of humiliation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messenger's curse is harsher than execution: it follows the cursed person in this life and the next, as in Islahi's comparison with Sabbath violators.
rows.anchor: the curse-punishment sticks to a person both in this world and in the

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses destroys the calf's statue and scatters its ashes to uproot polytheism and all its manifestations; the Prophet likewise destroyed idols at the conquest of Makkah.
rows.anchor: not only is it essential to wipe out polytheism, it is also essential to destroy all its manifestations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revelation brought by this prophet matches earlier revelation; rejecting it repeats the fate of nations that mocked and rejected their messengers.
rows.anchor: The reminder they needed for the conclusive communication of the truth has

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The universe is not amusement: its just, wise Creator will establish a day when truth prevails and falsehood is defeated.
rows.anchor: it is essential that He bring about a day in which the truth is victorious and falsehood is vanquished

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Multiple gods with separate wills would make the universe unsustainable; the prophets all taught monotheism, with no trace of polytheism in their teachings.
rows.anchor: If there had been multiple gods of this universe having their own will and intention, it would not have survived

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Angels are God's honourable servants, not daughters or autonomous intercessors; they speak only with His permission, and anyone claiming partnership with God faces Hell.
rows.anchor: Angels are not daughters of God; they are His honourable servants. They cannot even utter a word before Him without His permission

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The universe's evident signs already attest to God's providence, mercy, wisdom, justice, monotheism, and the Day of Judgement, so no new sign is needed.
rows.anchor: why do they not reflect on the ones which are present before them all the time

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mockers are reminded that the Prophet is neither superhuman nor wealthy, while their deities cannot save them when God seizes them.
rows.anchor: he neither is a super human nor a wealthy person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opponents' arrogance cannot stop the messenger's call from spreading through Makkah; revelation warns them, but they ignore it and will regret God's punishment.
rows.anchor: the call of the messenger which they are trying to subvert is reaching Makkah through its whereabouts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: From vv48–77 the text lists celebrated prophets in ascending order, beginning with Moses and Abraham; p92 continues that their message matches the Qur’an's.
rows.anchor: prophets like Moses (sws), Abraham (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accounts of David and Solomon invite Quraysh to gratitude; Job, Ishmael, Idrīs, and Dhū al-Kifl encourage the Prophet and oppressed companions to persevere for God's mercy.
rows.anchor: if they too persevere in the wake of hardships, God will also bless them with His mercy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah, Zacharias, John, Mary, and Jesus exemplify that no one can impede God's mercy when He wills to aid His servants; all means are in His control.
rows.anchor: when God wants to show mercy to His servants, none can impede His intentions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conclusion reassures the Prophet and companions that all prophets taught one message; they should persist and leave those who divided it to God, since late faith will not help.
rows.anchor: all prophets of God have taught the same message they are preaching

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only God's pious servants attain the Hereafter's success; judgement is near, and the Prophet ends by supplicating God to judge between him and his foes.
rows.anchor: a decisive declaration is made from the tongue of the Prophet (sws) that the time of judgement is at hand

none: English translation of verses 21:1-15 only; no commentary to record.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah opens without introduction because it completes the previous sūrah's warning; their opening and closing verses dovetail, a proximity discussed in the explanation of al-Tawbah.
rows.anchor: it actually is a completion of the subject of warning on which the previous sūrah ended

rows.speaker: Ibn ‘Abbās
rows.claim: “People” refers to the idolaters of Makkah; using a general term while they evade God's reminder conveys aversion and regret.
rows.anchor: the Idolaters of Makkah, as is the opinion of Ibn ‘Abbās (rta)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The near accountability is factual: after a messenger conclusively communicates truth, a nation has one option, faith; refusal brings destruction, and heedlessness with evasion compounds guilt.
rows.anchor: after conclusive communication of the truth, it is necessarily wiped out

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God repeatedly sends fresh reminders to awaken the heedless, but the Makkans mock each one instead of valuing it.
rows.anchor: in order to awaken them from their slumber of negligence, He has continued to send fresh reminders

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammatically, the phrase is a second accusative of state (ḥāl); the heart should reflect and receive reminders, but the heedless mock serious truths.
rows.anchor: a second accusative of state ( ḥāl). The implication is that the real task of the heart is to reflect and receive reminder

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh leaders secretly spread propaganda that Muhammad is merely human and his powerful recitation is magic, hoping to prevent the Qur’an influencing upright listeners.
rows.anchor: the propaganda of the Quraysh which they would spread in

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the conspirators unjust indicts their self-harm in sealing their intellect and their harm to others through deception.
rows.anchor: people who have been unjust to their souls by sealing their own intellectual powers and also being unjust to others by fooling them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Magic” means the revelation Muhammad recited: Arabs used the term for powerful discourse, whose eloquence opponents could not deny but explained away as verbal sorcery.
rows.anchor: The Arabs would regard all powerful and moving words and discourses as magic

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “with your open eyes” flatters listeners as superior and discerning so that they will resist the Prophet's influence.
rows.anchor: is meant to incite a sense of superiority in them: they are not simpletons

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet answers his opponents' mischief by entrusting it to the all-knowing Lord of the heavens and earth; their conspiracies are known, so God will rescue believers.
rows.anchor: wherever these conspiracies are being hatched, they were fully known to Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aḍghāth is the plural of ḍighth, a handful of dry and wet grass; the idiom means incoherent, ambiguous dreams unworthy of interpretation.
rows.anchor: The latter means a handful of dry and wet grass

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opponents escalated from calling revelation magic to calling it dreams, fabrication, and poetry, demanding a sign like earlier messengers; they claimed Muhammad misrepresented dreams as Gabriel's revelation.
rows.anchor: He sees wayward dreams. Whatever thoughts he has in his mind are seen by him in his dreams

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Modern anti-religious critics similarly cast doubt on revelation, though Islahi says they dress the old claim in a more polished philosophy.
rows.anchor: of current times are of the same opinion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opponents' claim that the Qur’an is fabricated means Muhammad concocted it and wrongly attributed it to God.
rows.anchor: they also regard this Qur’ān to be a concoction which the Prophet (sws) wrongly ascribes to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling Muhammad a poet implied that jinn inspired his words, reducing his revelation to the familiar compositions of Arab poets and orators.
rows.anchor: the Arabs were of the view that every great poet was accompanied with jinn who inspired him with poetry

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opponents were overwhelmed by the Qur’an's grandeur and knew its effect on the masses was hard to dispel, so they tried to downgrade it as human work.
rows.anchor: they were deeply over-awed by its splendour and majesty and had fully understood that it was difficult to dispense with this awe from the hearts of the masses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After “as earlier messengers were sent,” “signs” is elided because context supplies it; the opponents meant miracles or signs of punishment.
rows.anchor: indications. The implication is that when they would think

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an argues from the world, the self, human nature, and intellect; faith naturally comes through heart and intellect, while miracle-based belief or belief after a punishment sign has no value.
rows.anchor: the natural path that reaches faith is through the heart and intellect

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opponents falsely framed the Prophet's refusal to meet their sign-demand as proof that he was not God's messenger.
rows.anchor: since he was evading it, so he is falsely claiming to be a prophet of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse reassures Muhammad to ignore their stubbornness: as past sign-rejecting nations were destroyed, these people are destined for destruction and would not believe at another sign.
rows.anchor: They are showing the same obduracy and stubbornness which the doomed nations of the past showed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All earlier messengers were human and received revelation; prophethood is distinguished by revelation, not superhuman status.
rows.anchor: All messengers before Muḥammad (sws) were human beings as well

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address shifts from the Prophet to his adversaries; the People of the Book are witnesses because even Quraysh's supporters cannot deny prophetic history.
rows.anchor: Making them as witnesses was tantamount to making an enemy as witness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the People of the Book “men of knowledge” is rhetorically apt: those who remember prophetic history will affirm the fact despite hostility.
rows.anchor: those of them who remember the history of their prophets will not dare deny this fact

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “If you do not know” is sarcastic: Quraysh, Abraham and Ishmael's claimed descendants, know those patriarchs were human; if forgotten, they can ask the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: though they, as the progeny and claimants to Abraham’s religion, know that both Abraham (sws) and Ishmael (sws) were human beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets shared ordinary human traits, eating and dying; the cited objection that a human messenger must be rejected is refuted, including the claim that a messenger should be immortal.
rows.anchor: The words وَ ﻣَﺎ refute this claim of theirs that a messenger should be immortal

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's promise to messengers is that rejecting nations will be destroyed and believers saved; two punishments are warned, and this passage refers to the worldly one.
rows.anchor: Here the reference is to first of these torments

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The past promise was fulfilled; “those We want” makes the warning immediate for Quraysh, since only God chooses who survives and none can evade Him.
rows.anchor: even at this time they are facing this decisive phase

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Those who exceeded the limits” are obdurate rebels who break God's bounds and mock the messenger's warnings; rebels are punished.
rows.anchor: people who obdurately break the bounds of God and make fun of the warnings of the messenger

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Revelation has thoroughly reminded the Arabs before judgement, removing any excuse of ignorance; rejecting it brings the fate of earlier nations under God's unchanging practice.
rows.anchor: Now they cannot present the excuse before Him that they had not been reminded

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question “do you not understand?” is a severe rebuke for inviting doom; see the discussion of 20:133-145 to grasp the verse's emphasis.
rows.anchor: what has happened to the intellect of these foolish people; why are they calling for their doom

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier nations were destroyed for the same injustice of mocking God's reminder; God did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves by ignoring a messenger's warning in arrogance.
rows.anchor: God was not unjust to them; they inflicted injustice on their own selves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God can readily replace a rebellious nation; individuals and peoples should not treat themselves as indispensable, since heedlessness breeds self-importance.
rows.anchor: None should regard himself to be indispensable for this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Past nations arrogantly demanded punishment, then could neither avert it nor escape when it came; no one flees God's grasp.
rows.anchor: when the torment did visit them, they could do nothing to avert it and ran away from there

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to return to homes and resources is a vivid portrayal of God's grasp, forcing the doomed back to be questioned.
rows.anchor: It is as if God’s grasp itself is telling them
